correction.text: Syracuse 'founded by the Corinthians in 733 BC': the polis and its chora, a 25-km circle

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria has no Syracuse row; the page has no infobox area. The city's chora only; the page says it 'subjugated nearby territories' but names none before Gelon. Soft edges.

correction.text: Syracuse with Gelon's Gela and Camarina

keyframe_review.note: Gelon takes Syracuse in 485 and unites Gela and Camarina with it (ledger /1).

correction.text: Syracuse, Gela, Camarina, Euboea and Megara Hyblaea

keyframe_review.note: Euboea and Megara Hyblaea are conquered in 483. The pages say nothing of the later archaic and democratic reach (Hieron I, Thrasybulus, 478-405); the shape stays until Dionysius I's seizure of power in 405. Gelon's victory at Himera (480) with Theron of Acragas moves no border on the page.

correction.text: Dionysius I's Sicily: 'seized total power and became tyrant' in 405; the Greek east and the interior

keyframe_review.note: Siracusa, Ragusa, Catania, Messina and Caltanissetta provinces and a 35-km circle round Enna, the researcher's reading of the 'Greek east and the interior' (the page names no city; the Carthaginians kept at least a third of Sicily). Soft edges.

correction.text: Sicily with the Adriatic colonies: Ancona (387), Adria and Lissos (385), Issa

keyframe_review.note: One-year keyframe: the Adriatic discs are the colonies of 387-385.

correction.text: Sicily, the Adriatic colonies and Rhegium: 'he took Rhegium in 386'

keyframe_review.note: Rhegium joins in 386; Dionysius I's war with Carthage (397-392) is a contest in the west, outside this shape.
The Italian and Adriatic holdings are dropped at 367 (bridge, confidence 1: the Dionysius II page names only Locri).

correction.text: the core of Syracuse: Siracusa, Ragusa and Catania provinces

keyframe_review.note: After Dion's return in 357 'Other Sicilian cities broke away and were ruled by local tyrants'; Timoleon arrives in 344, Dionysius II surrenders the citadel (344), Agathocles' coup follows in 317.

correction.text: the east and the interior under Agathocles

keyframe_review.note: Agathocles 'quickly brought many cities and fortresses under his control' after the peace of 314/313 and took Messina in 313/312.
Defeated at the Himera River and besieged in Syracuse in 311; the African expedition runs from August 310 to 307.

correction.text: 'Sicily east of the Halycus River' (306 treaty)

keyframe_review.note: 'A peace treaty with Carthage left him in control of Sicily east of the Halycus River' (306); king of Sicily in 304.

correction.text: the core of Syracuse after Agathocles

keyframe_review.note: The interior and the north coast go to Carthage at 289 (bridge, confidence 1); Pyrrhus holds Syracuse in 278-276 (occupation, same shape); Hiero II rules from 275.

correction.text: the south-east of Sicily and the eastern coast as far as Tauromenium: Roman ally

keyframe_review.note: The treaty of 263 limits Hiero to the south-east and the east coast and makes him a Roman ally, so the renderer tints the land (vassal_start 263, vassal_end 215, matching roman-republic /ledger/36 and /61).

correction.text: Syracuse under Hieronymus and the anti-Roman faction

keyframe_review.note: Same shape, again independent and at war with Rome from 214 until the fall of the city in the autumn of 212.

region.text: Syracuse and its chora

ledger.note: 733 BC: Syracuse 'founded by the Corinthians in 733 BC (according to the Thucydidean dating)'.

region.text: Gela and Camarina: Gelon, lord of Gela, takes Syracuse in 485 and 'removed all the aristocracy from Camarina'; Gela is left to his brother Hiero

ledger.note: 485 BC: 'In 485 BC, the aristocracy of Syracuse called the Gamori' sought Gelon's aid and he took the city 'with little or no resistance' (tyrant 485-478); his lands, Gela and, by the page's 491 account, Camarina, join the city: 'forced half the citizens of Gela to move to Syracuse'. Naxos and Zancle, named in the same 491 sentence, are not drawn (the sentence is about territory 'included' under Gelon before Syracuse). The discs are my reading.

region.text: Megara Hyblaea and Euboea: 'he conquered nearby Euboea and Megara Hyblaea (483 BC)', removing the aristocracy and enslaving the rest

ledger.note: 483 BC: Gelon conquers Euboea and Megara Hyblaea; their land joins Syracuse.

region.text: Sicily east of the Halycus (Platani): the Greek east and the interior to Enna

ledger.note: 405 BC: Dionysius I 'seized total power and became tyrant' (tyrant 405-367). He 'fought a war with Carthage from 397 BC to 392 BC with mixed success'; at his death the Carthaginians 'were still masters of at least a third of' Sicily, which leaves the Greek east and the interior to Syracuse. The pages do not name Naxos, Catana or Leontini, so the extent is inferred (confidence 1). Before 405 the Gelon page gives the archaic reach (485, 483), added as gains.

region.text: the Carthaginian west of Sicily (Motya, Trapani province, the zone of the carthage dossier; the Dionysius I page names no place)

ledger.note: 397 BC: Dionysius I 'fought a war with Carthage from 397 BC to 392 BC with mixed success' (the carthage dossier has -398 to -393, one year earlier on both ends).

region.text: the Carthaginian west of Sicily (the zone of the carthage dossier)

ledger.note: 392 BC: the war with Carthage ends; at Dionysius' death in 367 the Carthaginians 'were still masters of at least a third' of Sicily.

region.text: the Adriatic colonies: Ancona, Adria, Lissos and Issa

ledger.note: 387-385 BC: the Adriatic. Ancona 'a colony populated in 387 BC by political exiles', 'Lissos (in 385 BC, now Lezhë)', 'Adria (in 385 BC, now Adria)', Issa undated; 'Around 387-385 BC'.

region.text: Rhegium

ledger.note: 386 BC: 'he took Rhegium in 386 and sold the inhabitants as slaves'; the 387 expedition 'devastated the territories of Thurii and Croton'.

union.text: the Adriatic colonies: Ancona, Adria, Lissos and Issa

region.text: Rhegium and the Adriatic colonies

ledger.note: 367 BC: Dionysius I dies; the pages say nothing of the Italian and Adriatic holdings under Dionysius II, Dion and Timoleon ('his rule lasted about a decade'), so Rhegium and the colonies are dropped at his death rather than carried blindly. Confidence 1. Dionysius II page (opened 2026-10-19): the page names no Italian or Adriatic holding but Locri, where he was tyrant after his expulsion (356-346); still a bridge (confidence 1).
367 BC: Dionysius II succeeds: 'When his father died in 367 BC' (tyrant 367-357, again 346-344; the page's infobox has 367-356).

region.text: the Sicilian cities outside Syracuse broke away: 'Other Sicilian cities broke away and were ruled by local tyrants' after Dion's return in 357

ledger.note: 357 BC: Dion returns and Dionysius II loses Syracuse; 'Other Sicilian cities broke away and were ruled by local tyrants', so the Sicilian holdings beyond the core (Messina, the interior) leave Syracuse; the page infobox has 356 for the end of the tyranny.
317 BC: 'In 317 BC, Agathocles used this force to launch a coup' (tyrant 317-289).

region.text: 'quickly brought many cities and fortresses under his control'; Agathocles took Messina in 313/312 BC; Tauromenium also came under his control

ledger.note: c. 313 BC: after the peace of 314/313 Agathocles 'quickly brought many cities and fortresses under his control' and took Messina in 313/312 'without a fight'; the cities opposed to him were Acragas, Gela and Messina. The region is my reading (the page does not list his cities).

region.text: the interior and the north coast: Enna, the Nebrodi, the Himera valleys

ledger.note: 311-306 BC: Agathocles' war with Carthage 'between 311 and 306 BC', with the 'expedition to Africa' (Syracuse page).

region.text: the Sicilian holdings beyond the core after the Himera River: 'Agathocles was defeated in the Battle of the Himera River and besieged in Syracuse'

ledger.note: 311 BC: 'In 311 BC Agathocles was defeated in the Battle of the Himera River and besieged in Syracuse' (mirror of carthage /ledger/14, Hamilcar wins the rest of Sicily); he lands in Africa in August 310. The page does not say which cities went over; the ring is my reading.

region.text: the interior and the north coast: Enna, the Nebrodi, the Himera valleys

ledger.note: 306 BC: 'A peace treaty with Carthage left him in control of Sicily east of the Halycus River.'

region.text: Sicily east of the Halycus, regained: Messina and the interior of Caltanissetta (the core of Siracusa, Ragusa and Catania was never lost)

ledger.note: 306 BC: Sicily east of the Halycus confirmed to Syracuse; Tauromenium 'also fell into his hands'. Drawn as a confirmation of the eastern two-thirds. With the loss of 311 added, the gain is the ring only (Messina, Caltanissetta and the interior), not the whole of the east.
304 BC: Agathocles 'styled himself king of Sicily in 304 BC'.

region.text: the interior and the north coast: Enna, the Nebrodi, the Himera valleys

ledger.note: 289 BC: Agathocles dies; the Agathocles page 'gives no account of what happened to Syracuse's territory after 289 BC'. By 278 the Carthaginians were besieging Syracuse itself and in 277 'Carthage kept only Lilybaeum and its environs' after Pyrrhus' campaign, so the interior had changed hands twice. The interior and north coast are given to Carthage here at confidence 1; the Mamertines held Messana from 288 (their own dossier). The Hicetas page (opened 2026-10-19) is the Pythagorean philosopher, not the tyrant, and is silent; the loss stays a bridge (confidence 1). The loss of -263 repeats the same ring (Hiero's treaty limit), see notes.

region.text: south-eastern Sicily and the east coast to Tauromenium

ledger.note: 278 BC: 'Late 278: Pyrrhus entered Syracuse after the Carthaginians abandoned their siege'; Syracuse a belligerent on his side 'from 278'. Hatched for Pyrrhus until 'Early 276: He returned to southern Italy'.

region.text: south-eastern Sicily and the east coast to Tauromenium

ledger.note: 276 BC: Pyrrhus leaves Sicily.

275 BC: Hiero II. 'Between 275 and 271 BC he seized total power in Syracuse by allying with the demos' (reign 275-215); 'proclaimed king after a victory in 265 BC' (the Mamertines page has him king after the Longanus 'In around 270 BC').

region.text: the Mylae plain and the Messana hinterland

ledger.note: c. 270-264 BC: the Mamertine war. Hiero 'defeated the Mamertines in a pitched battle near Mylae along the Longanus river'; he besieged Messana in 265 until a Carthaginian fleet 'occupied the harbour of Messina'.

region.text: the Messana country

ledger.note: 264 BC: Hiero 'joined the Carthaginian leader Hanno', the fighting with Appius Claudius Caudex 'was inconclusive, and Hiero withdrew to Syracuse'.

region.text: the interior and north coast beyond Tauromenium

ledger.note: 263 BC: the Roman treaty. Under it Hiero 'would rule the south-east of Sicily and the eastern coast as far as Tauromenium'; the roman-republic dossier draws the alliance (vassal_start syracuse 263, vassal_end 215). Whatever Syracuse still claimed beyond Tauromenium and the south-east passes to the Roman war zone. Hiero II page: 'in 263 he concluded a treaty with Rome, by which he was to rule over the south-east of Sicily and the eastern coast as far as Tauromenium'; 'Until his death he remained loyal to the Romans'.

region.text: the south-east of Sicily and the eastern coast as far as Tauromenium

ledger.note: 263 BC: 'in 263 he concluded a treaty with Rome, by which he was to rule over the south-east of Sicily and the eastern coast as far as Tauromenium'; 'Until his death he remained loyal to the Romans' (vassal_start syracuse 263 in roman-republic).
215 BC: 'Hieronymus came to the throne in 215 BC after his grandfather's death, and Syracuse fell under an anti-Roman faction'.

region.text: the south-east of Sicily and the eastern coast as far as Tauromenium

ledger.note: 215 BC: Hiero II dies and 'Hieronymus came to the throne in 215 BC after his grandfather's death, and Syracuse fell under an anti-Roman faction'; the Hiero II page gives both 215 and 'shortly after the Battle of Cannae in 216'.

region.text: south-eastern Sicily and the east coast to Tauromenium

ledger.note: 214-212 BC: 'War broke out in 214 BC'; Epicydes and Hippocrates 'had retaken the city and named themselves tyrants'; Marcellus 'laid siege to the port city by sea and land in 213 BC' ('Spring 213 - Autumn 212 BC').

region.text: south-eastern Sicily and the east coast to Tauromenium

ledger.note: 212 BC (autumn): the fall. A night raid during a festival of Artemis took the outer city; after eight months Moeriscus 'opened a gate near the Fountains of Arethusa' and 'Marcellus then gave Syracuse to plunder'; Archimedes killed. Rome 'united the whole of Sicily as a Roman province by 210 BC'.

region.text: south-eastern Sicily and the east coast to Tauromenium

notes: New state (the brief: Cliopatria lacks Syracuse; its land sits in the Greek City-States umbrella). Drawn as the city 733-405, as Sicily east of the Halycus under Dionysius I (with Rhegium and the Adriatic colonies 387-367) and Agathocles (306 peace), as the south-east with the east coast to Tauromenium under Hiero II (the 263 treaty), and as a Roman ally 263-215 (tint from roman-republic). Low-confidence choices: the 405 extent, the 367 drop of the Italian and Adriatic holdings, the 289 loss of the interior to Carthage. The Dionysius page's Rhegium date is 386 (not 387). Wikidata Q13670 is the city's id (unverified). Gazetteer: Enna province, Tauromenium/Taormina, Lissos/Lezhë, Issa/Vis absent (circles used). Revised 2026-10-19 after review: keyframes added; vassal_start 263 and vassal_end 215 (Hiero II page, Siege of Syracuse page) match roman-republic /ledger/36 and /61; loss to carthage of 311 added (Agathocles page; mirror of carthage /ledger/14), the 306 gain is now the ring only; contest 397-392 added from the Dionysius I page (carthage has -398 to -393, one year earlier on both ends); counterpart 'Kingdom of Epirus (Pyrrhus)' in the wars list replaced by kingdom-of-epirus. Thin items: Gelon page opened, so gains at 485 (Gela and Camarina) and 483 (Euboea, Megara Hyblaea) are added; Dionysius II page opened: it names no Italian or Adriatic holding but Locri and says other Sicilian cities broke away in 357, so a loss in 357 (nobody) and a gain in 313 (Agathocles took Messina 313/312 and many cities) are added; the Hicetas page is the philosopher's and the 289 loss stays a bridge. Inconsistency left in place: the 289 loss gives the ring to Carthage (confidence 1) and the 263 loss to Rome takes the same ring again. Gazetteer lacks Gela, Camarina, Megara Hyblaea (coordinates used). The pages differ on the end of Hiero II (215 or shortly after Cannae, 216) and of Dionysius II's first tyranny (357 or 356). Wikidata Q13670 could not be checked and is set to null.
